title: Speaking for the women
hookLine: he asks the Buddha whether women can awaken, and the answer is yes (Vinaya, Cullavagga 10)

cards: Early on this path, we stood outside a hall at Vesali with Mahapajapati and the women who had walked there, dusty and in tears, to ask to be ordained. We heard Ananda go in for them.

Today we stay with Ananda: the exact question he asked, what came back, and what it cost him much later. The Vinaya, the monks' own rulebook, keeps all three. A request has been turned down three times.
Ananda decides not to ask the same thing a fourth time. He asks something else.

teach.b: Ananda stops asking whether women may go forth, and asks whether they can. In paraphrase: Lord, if a woman goes forth into the homeless life, is she able to realize the fruits of the path, even full awakening?
It's a question about ability, not permission. Second, the answer. Yes, Ananda.
They are able. That yes is written into the Vinaya itself. Then Ananda speaks for one woman in particular.

Mahapajapati, he reminds the Buddha, was the Buddha's own aunt and foster mother, who nursed him and fed him after his mother died. And the Buddha agrees to ordain women, with eight special rules. Third, the garland.

Ananda carries the rules out to Mahapajapati, and she answers with a picture, in paraphrase: as a young person who has just bathed would take a garland of flowers in both hands and set it on their own head, so I take these rules.
Buddhists today read that moment in different ways. Some hear grace in her acceptance. Others question the rules themselves and their history.

Both readings are part of the conversation now. Fourth, the cost. After the Buddha's death, at a gathering of elders, Ananda is charged with faults, and one of them is that he worked to have women ordained.
His answer, in paraphrase: I did it because Mahapajapati had nursed the Blessed One. I don't see it as a fault. But out of respect for you, I confess it.
He confessed, and didn't pretend he had changed his mind.
Speaking up for someone can be counted against you long after.

how: In Buddhist tradition Mahapajapati is remembered as the first nun, and Ananda as the one who spoke up for the women.

o: Ananda's sister, who asked to be a nun
the Buddha's aunt and foster mother, first nun
the Buddha's birth mother, who died young

games.q: speaking for the women: tap the pairs.
p: takes the rules like a garland
count his pleading as a fault

s: the Buddha's yes was about whether women were allowed in
Ananda asked whether women are able to realize awakening, and the answer was yes.
Mahapajapati compared accepting the rules to setting a garland on her head
like someone freshly bathed taking a garland of flowers.
after the Buddha's death the elders praised Ananda for pleading for the women
they counted it as a fault; he said he saw none, but confessed out of respect.

games.q: you're Ananda. the Buddha has died, and the elders say your pleading for the women's ordination was a fault. what do you do?
o: deny you ever pleaded for them.
say you see no fault, but confess out of respect.
games.why: he explains that Mahapajapati had nursed the Buddha, says he doesn't see it as a fault, and confesses it out of respect for the elders.

practice: Think of a room where things get decided, at work, in your family, in a group you belong to, and one person who isn't heard there.
Silently shape one plain question, like Ananda's, that asks what's true about them rather than what's allowed, and rest with the breath, noticing how it sits.

wordCard.voice: Mahapajapati. The Buddha's aunt and foster mother, for whom Ananda pleaded, the first woman ordained, who took the eight special rules like a garland.

orig.note: Pali: arahantship, full awakening; what Ananda asked whether women could realize.

carryVoice: Your line: women can awaken. The answer was yes, and the Vinaya kept it. See you tomorrow.
